headline: Password Activity — Secret Word Speaking Game for ESL Classes
outcomes: Students produce the target word naturally in conversation rather than reciting definitions — the difference between knowing a word and using it
Build speaking spontaneity: the game requires fluid, on-the-fly sentence construction rather than planned output
Develop listening comprehension and inference skills as students decode conversational cues without a direct reveal
Practise the pragmatic skill of managing information — what you say, how much you say, and when to stay vague
howItWorks: The AI assigns a secret word to each team — only they can see it on their devices
Team members try to work the word naturally into conversation without saying it directly or obviously
Other teams listen and try to identify the secret word from context clues
Points are scored for successfully using the word naturally and for correctly identifying other teams' passwords
teacherUseCases: Post-vocabulary input production practice — run Password after introducing a new word set to push students from passive recognition into active use
Speaking assessment alternative — observe which students can use words flexibly in context, not just recall them in isolation
Review game — assign password words drawn from the lesson's key vocabulary list to build natural usage before the end of class

faq.q: How do students 'say the word naturally'?
faq.a: Students try to embed the password word into a conversation sentence as if it came up organically — for example, if the word is 'ambitious', they might say 'My older brother is so ambitious, he works until midnight every night.' The challenge is making it sound unplanned.

faq.q: What stops a student from just saying the word directly?
faq.a: The teacher monitors for obvious reveals — saying the exact word, spelling it, or giving a dictionary definition counts as a violation and nullifies the points. The buzz button lets the teacher flag violations the moment they happen.

faq.q: How are the password words chosen?
faq.a: The AI selects words from the lesson topic matched to the difficulty level — concrete nouns and common verbs for lower levels, abstract or collocational vocabulary for higher levels. You can regenerate the word set or type your own words before starting.

faq.q: Can a team pass if they can't think of a sentence?
faq.a: Yes — teams can skip their turn without penalty. The game continues to the next team. Passing too many times reduces scoring opportunity but keeps the class moving.

Teams earn points for each natural use of their password word that the teacher approves, plus points for correctly guessing another team's word. Speed matters — the first team to guess correctly scores highest.
